newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upper house rejects Waigel's tax reform.
newsitem.headline: German upper house rejects Waigel's tax reform.

text.p: Germany's opposition-controlled upper house of parliament, or Bundesrat, on Friday rejected Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax reforms for 1998 and 1999, sending the bills to parliament's mediation committee.

The majority of states controlled by the Social Democrats (SPD) criticised the federal government's tax legislation as socially unjust and said federal, state and local goverments could not accept a 45 billion mark ($26 billion) financing gap caused by tax cuts contained in the bills.

"We are prepared to reach an agreement," said Henning Voscherau, Hamburg mayor and SPD negotiator in tax talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition. "But not at any price. I will not hold out my hand for the ruination of my budget."
The 1998 and 1999 tax bills, which envisage net tax cuts of 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion), last week passed comfortably in the lower house.

The anticipated rejection of the legislation by the upper house sends the bills to the mediation committee which is made up of 32 members equally divided between the Bundesrat and the lower house, or Bundestag.
The tax reform, which was amended in committee, would cut the lowest rate of income tax to 15 percent in 1999 from 39 percent while the top rate would fall to 39 percent from 53.

The solidarity income tax surcharge, raised to help rebuild ex-communist eastern Germany, would fall by two points to 5.5 percent next year. The top rate of corporation tax would fall in two steps to 35 percent by 1999 from 45 percent now.
Waigel defended the tax cuts and urged the SPD to end its reform blockade in the interest of jobs and economic growth.
"The mere agreement on a comprehensive, workable (tax) concept would stimulate the economy," he said.
"Economic fundamentals are in order, interest rates are low, prices are stable. Why, then, is unemployment rising in spite of economic recovery?"
Waigel said structural problems afflicted the economy and these could only be addressed by broad fiscal reform.

"The last tax estimate showed that lost tax revenue was only partially caused by cyclical economic factors. The rest was structural," he said. "Improvements in taxation would raise profitability for companies and bring an investment boost."
But Voscherau said that while German companies complained of high taxation, many of the country's blue-chip firms took advantage of loopholes and paid little or no tax.
"Whoever achieves record corporate profits and pays 20 to 30 percent in taxes and then badmouths the Fatherland because of high tax rates is a liar and is just poisoning the well," said Voscherau.
